1239935.overview:
### Impact

Multer's `diskStorage` can leave complete, orphaned files on disk when a multipart upload is aborted in the brief window before the storage engine assigns the file path. This is an incomplete fix of CVE-2026-5038: the earlier cleanup removes only in-flight uploads that already have a path, so an upload aborted inside that window is written to disk with nothing left to remove it, and the application is not given a handle to clean it up. An unauthenticated attacker sending aborted requests to any route backed by disk storage can accumulate orphaned files until the upload directory or the shared system temporary directory is exhausted. An asynchronous `destination` or `filename` widens the window.

### Patches

Users should upgrade to `2.4.0` or higher.

### Workarounds

None.
1239935.title: multer vulnerable to Denial of Service via orphaned disk writes on aborted uploads

1239942.overview:
### Impact

`fast-uri` serializes the `port` component of a URI without validating it. When recomposing the authority, `fast-uri` escapes the userinfo and host components but concatenates the port verbatim, so a `port` value that is not a sequence of digits can inject authority delimiters. For example, serializing a component whose `port` is `@127.0.0.1:8124` produces `http://trusted.example:@127.0.0.1:8124/app`, demoting the intended host to userinfo and pointing the authority at an attacker-controlled host. Both `fast-uri` and Node's `URL` read the result back as the attacker's host with no error, so re-validating the built URI does not catch it.

This affects applications that build URIs from parts and assign untrusted data to the `port` component (for example a fixed host from configuration and a port taken from user input or a service record). The same path is reachable through `serialize()`, `normalize()`, and `equal()` in their object forms. A `port` obtained from `parse()` is always digits and is not affected.

### Patches

This vulnerability has been patched in fast-uri `4.1.4`, `3.1.7`, and `2.4.6`. `recomposeAuthority` now rejects any port that is not `*DIGIT` per RFC 3986. All users should upgrade.

### Workarounds

If upgrading is not immediately possible, validate the `port` value against the RFC 3986 grammar (digits only) before passing a component to `serialize()`, `normalize()`, or `equal()`, and reject anything else, for example `if (!/^\d*$/.test(String(port))) throw new Error('invalid port')`.
1239942.title: fast-uri vulnerable to authority injection via an unvalidated port in serialize

1239945.overview:
### Impact

`fast-uri` accepts a host that contains an unbalanced or misplaced authority bracket (`[` or `]`) without reporting an error. A host that starts with `[` but does not end with `]`, such as `[@127.0.0.1`, is neither validated as an IP literal nor canonicalized as a domain name, so `parse()` returns it as the host with `error` undefined, while Node's `URL` (and `http.get`, `axios`, `got`, and other clients built on it) resolve the same string to `127.0.0.1`. An application that reads `parse().host` to make a host decision (an SSRF denylist, a redirect allowlist, or proxy routing) and then passes the original URL to an HTTP client evaluates its policy against a string that is not the host the request reaches. The same host is carried through `normalize()`, `equal()`, and `resolve()`.

### Patches

This vulnerability has been patched in fast-uri `4.1.4`, `3.1.7`, and `2.4.6`. `parse()` now reports `URI host is malformed.` for any host that contains a bracket but is not a valid `[IPv6]` literal. All users should upgrade.

### Workarounds

If upgrading is not immediately possible, reject any URL whose host contains a `[` or `]` that is not a well-formed IPv6 literal before making a host decision. Clients that fail closed on credential-bearing URLs, such as Node's global `fetch()`, are not affected by the reported vector.
1239945.title: fast-uri vulnerable to host confusion via an unclosed bracket in the URI authority

1240090.overview:
### Impact

`fast-uri` folds the host to lowercase before it percent-decodes the host, so a percent-encoded uppercase unreserved octet such as `%41` decodes to a literal `A` that is never folded. For a scheme-relative reference (`//host`) there is no scheme, so the host canonicalization that repairs this on a scheme-bearing URL does not run. As a result `parse`, `normalize`, and `equal` disagree on the same host: `parse("//%41.com").host` returns `"A.com"` while `parse("//a.com").host` and `parse("//A.com").host` return `"a.com"`, and `equal("//%41.com", "//a.com")` is `false` even though `equal("//A.com", "//a.com")` is `true`. An application that makes a case-sensitive host decision on `fast-uri` output for a scheme-relative reference, for example a host allowlist or denylist that compares `parse(url).host` or uses `fast-uri.equal`, can be steered past the check with a percent-encoded uppercase octet. Because a hostname is case-insensitive in DNS and HTTP routing, the evading spelling reaches the same host the check meant to gate, so the effect is check evasion rather than reaching a different registrable host.

### Patches

Upgrade to `fast-uri` 4.1.5, 3.1.8, or 2.4.7.

### Workarounds

Compare hosts case-insensitively (lowercase the parsed host before any allowlist or denylist decision), or avoid making case-sensitive host decisions on scheme-relative input until upgrading.
1240090.title: fast-uri vulnerable to inconsistent host case normalization via percent-encoded octets

1240093.overview:
### Impact

`fast-uri`'s `mailto` scheme parser compares each query field name to the reserved names (`to`, `subject`, `body`) while the name is still percent-encoded, and only percent-decodes it when storing it as a generic header. On serialize, the decoded name is re-emitted, so a field name such as `%74o` (percent-encoded `to`) is not recognized as a recipient at parse time (`parse().to` shows only the legitimate recipient) but materializes as a literal `to=` field after `serialize()`, and reparsing then treats it as a recipient. The same technique smuggles `subject` and `body` through `%73ubject` and `%62ody`.

An application that parses an untrusted mailto URI, makes a display, allowlist, or logging decision on `parse().to`, then re-serializes the result and passes the serialized string to a mail client or an outbound send path can gain an attacker-chosen recipient, subject, or body that was not visible when the recipient list was checked. A scanner inspecting the raw input for an extra `to=` sees nothing, because the injected field appears only after `fast-uri` serializes.

### Patches

Upgrade to `fast-uri` 4.1.5.

### Workarounds

Percent-decode and compare mailto field names case-insensitively before trusting `parse().to`, or re-check the recipient list on the serialized output rather than only on the initial parse, until upgrading.
1240093.title: fast-uri vulnerable to mailto header injection via percent-encoded field-name desynchronization

1240097.title: ip-address: isInSubnet() and isHostInSubnet() compare addresses of different families as if they shared an address space, allowing an allowlist check to admit an address outside its range

1240098.title: ip-address: Address6 builds a parse diagnostic proportional to the input with no length bound, allowing a single long string to stall or crash the process

1240103.overview:
### Summary

Expanding `{a},b}`-shaped input takes time quadratic in the number of literal `}` characters, blocking the event loop.

Bash preserves a quirk where a brace group followed by a comma set still expands (`{a},b}`). The parser implements this by rewriting the string and restarting the scan. Each pass absorbs exactly one `}` and re-scans from the beginning, so `n` trailing braces cost `n` full passes.

### Reproduction

```js
const build = n => '{a}' + '}'.repeat(n) + ',z}'

for (const n of [8000, 16000, 32000, 64000, 128000]) {
  const t = Date.now()
  expand(build(n))
  console.log(n, Date.now() - t + 'ms')
}
```

| n | input | time | results |
|---|---|---|---|
| 8,000 | 8 KB | 110 ms | 2 |
| 16,000 | 16 KB | 446 ms | 2 |
| 32,000 | 32 KB | 1.7 s | 2 |
| 64,000 | 64 KB | 6.9 s | 2 |
| 128,000 | 128 KB | **27.7 s** | 2 |

`ms/n^2` is flat at ~1.7 and each doubling of `n` costs exactly 4.0x - quadratic. 128 KB of input blocks the event loop for nearly half a minute to produce two results.

### Mechanism

Instrumenting the rewrite branch confirms it runs exactly `n + 1` times, once per literal `}`, each re-scanning the whole string.

There is a second multiplier. The rewrite replaces the group's closing `}` with the internal `escClose` sentinel, which is `'\0CLOSE' + Math.random() + '\0'` - about 25 characters. The working string therefore *grows* by ~25 characters on every pass:

| n | input length | final string length |
|---|---|---|
| 1,000 | 1,006 | 26,006 |
| 8,000 | 8,006 | 208,006 |

So the input is inflated roughly 26x, and that factor multiplies both the quadratic constant and peak memory. This makes it partly a memory-pressure issue as well as a CPU one.

### Why `max` and `maxLength` do not help

The cost is in parsing, before the result set exists. The payload yields 2 results regardless of size, so neither bound is ever reached.

### Impact

An application passing an untrusted pattern to `expand()`, directly or through `minimatch` / `glob`, can have its event loop blocked for tens of seconds by a payload well under minimatch's 65,536-character cap. For a single-threaded Node server that is a full stall, not just a slow request.

Degraded availability rather than a crash - the process recovers once the expansion completes.

### Affected versions

Verified affected on 1.1.18, 2.1.4, 3.0.6 and 5.0.9, all within a few percent of each other (~460-490 ms at n=16,000).

### Patch

The rewrite loop gets an iteration bound. Past the cap the remaining string is treated as non-expanding and returned literally, consistent with the existing `max` / `maxLength` caps, which truncate rather than throw.

Note this bounds the number of passes, not the cost of each: worst-case work remains proportional to `cap x input length`. The cap is set low enough that the residual is bounded in practice, and far above what any realistic `{a},b}` input needs.

### Severity note

Scored 5.3 Medium (`A:L`) for consistency with GHSA-3jxr-9vmj-r5cp, the other algorithmic-complexity advisory on this package (CWE-407), which uses the same vector. The stack-exhaustion advisories on this package score `A:H` because they crash the process outright; this one stalls it.
1240103.title: brace-expansion: Quadratic-time expansion of the `{a},b}` rewrite causes CPU denial of service

1240107.overview:
### Summary

`expand_()` recurses once per level of brace *nesting*. Deeply nested input exhausts the native stack and crashes the process.

This is distinct from CVE-2026-14257 / GHSA-mh99-v99m-4gvg, which made the *tail* iterative (recursion on `m.post`, driven by how many groups are chained). Nesting depth drives a different recursion that the tail fix never touched, so the documented constant-stack-depth guarantee only ever covered chained input, not nested input.

It is also distinct from GHSA-6j4f-fj2g-mc7p, which fixed recursion in `parseCommaParts()`. Both payloads below still crash with that fix applied.

### Two recursion sites

**Comma members.** Each alternative of a brace set is expanded by a recursive call, so nesting a set inside every alternative recurses once per level:

```js
expand('{a,'.repeat(4000) + 'z' + '}'.repeat(4000))
// RangeError: Maximum call stack size exceeded
```

Crashes at depth 3,907 - about **15.6 KB** of input.

**Single set.** A brace set whose body parses to a single part is expanded by a recursive call before being re-wrapped (`x{{a,b}}y` -> `x{a}y x{b}y`), which recurses once per nesting level:

```js
expand('{'.repeat(3200) + 'a,b' + '}'.repeat(3200))
// RangeError: Maximum call stack size exceeded
```

Crashes at depth 3,125 - about **6.25 KB** of input. This is the cheapest stack-exhaustion payload known against this package: roughly a quarter the input of GHSA-6j4f-fj2g-mc7p (29 KB), and about a tenth of minimatch's `MAX_PATTERN_LENGTH` (65,536).

### Why `max` and `maxLength` do not help

Both crashes happen while recursing into sub-expansions, before the result set grows. The payloads produce almost no output - the single-set case yields 2 results - so neither bound is ever the limiter. `expand(payload, { max: 1, maxLength: 1 })` still overflows.

### Impact

Any application passing an untrusted string to `expand()`, directly or through `minimatch` / `glob` as a user-supplied glob pattern, can be crashed. In Node a `RangeError` the application does not catch terminates the process, so a server globbing user input is exposed to remote unauthenticated denial of service.

Availability only. No code execution, no data exposure.

### Affected versions

Verified affected on 1.1.18, 2.1.4, 3.0.6 and 5.0.9, at near-identical depths on every line (single set: 3,125 on all four; comma members: 3,907-4,102). Not a regression from any recent fix - the gap predates them.

### Patch

A `maxDepth` bound (default `EXPANSION_MAX_DEPTH`) is threaded through `expand_()`. Past the cap a group is treated as non-expanding and returned literally, which is how the parser already handles a group that cannot expand. This matches the existing `max` / `maxLength` caps, which truncate rather than throw, so `expand()` continues never to throw on any input.

The default sits far above any realistic nesting depth and well below the crash threshold.
1240107.title: brace-expansion: DoS via uncontrolled recursion on nested brace groups causing stack exhaustion

1240111.overview:
### Summary

`parseCommaParts()` can exhaust the native stack and crash the process. There are two distinct ways to trigger it, both reachable from a single untrusted pattern string.

This is the parsing-side counterpart to CVE-2026-14257 / GHSA-mh99-v99m-4gvg. That fix made `expand_()` iterative and documented a constant-stack-depth guarantee, but `parseCommaParts()` was left recursive, so the guarantee only held for one of the two parsing paths.

### Vector 1 - unbounded recursion on `post`

`parseCommaParts()` recursed on the remainder of the string once per brace group:

```js
const postParts = parseCommaParts(post)   // unbounded
```

A brace group containing many comma-separated groups drives one recursion level per group:

```js
expand('{' + '{a},'.repeat(7000) + 'b}')
// RangeError: Maximum call stack size exceeded
```

About 7,300 repetitions - roughly 29 KB of input - is enough on Node 24; roughly 6,300 (25 KB) on Node 18. The threshold is identical on every affected release line.

### Vector 2 - `push.apply` with an unbounded array

Even with the recursion removed, `parseCommaParts()` spread whole arrays into an argument list:

```js
p.push.apply(p, postParts)
parts.push.apply(parts, p)
```

`Function.prototype.apply` places one argument per element on the stack, so a single large array overflows it. This needs **no recursion depth at all** - the following reaches a recursion depth of exactly 1:

```js
expand('{{x},' + 'a,'.repeat(125000) + 'b}')
// RangeError: Maximum call stack size exceeded
```

Threshold is about 124,300 repetitions (~249 KB). This vector was not part of the original report; it was found while verifying the fix. A patch that only de-recurses but keeps `push.apply` leaves a working denial of service behind.

### Why `max` and `maxLength` do not help

Both crashes happen during **parsing**, before any expansion. The payloads produce one result per group, so output size grows linearly with input and is never the limiter. `expand(payload, { max: 1, maxLength: 1 })` still overflows.

### Impact

Any application that passes an untrusted string to `expand()` - directly, or through `minimatch` / `glob` where it is a user-supplied glob pattern - can be crashed. In Node, a `RangeError` that the application does not catch terminates the process, so a server that globs user input is exposed to remote unauthenticated denial of service.

`minimatch`'s own `MAX_PATTERN_LENGTH` cap (65,536) does not help against vector 1: the overflow threshold sits well below it. Confirmed on minimatch 10.2.6 - a 64,003-byte pattern passes the length check and overflows both `minimatch.braceExpand()` and `new minimatch.Minimatch()`.

This is an availability-only issue. No code execution and no data exposure.

### Not a regression

5.0.8 and 5.0.9 overflow at the same repetition count, so the gap predates the recent advisories; those fixes simply did not reach it. Verified affected on 1.1.18, 2.1.4, 3.0.6, 5.0.8 and 5.0.9, all at an identical threshold.

### Patch

`parseCommaParts()` is rewritten as a loop that carries the partial part across chunks, and every array append uses an element-by-element loop rather than `push.apply`. The redundant `if (!str) return ['']` guard is dropped - the loop returns `['']` for the empty string on its own.

Equivalence of the old and new implementations was checked by differential testing: exhaustive over every string of `{`, `}`, `,`, `a` up to length 7 plus 300,000 random inputs - 322,000 cases, zero mismatches.

### Severity note

Scored 7.5 High under CVSS 3.1 for consistency with the other availability advisories on this package (GHSA-mh99-v99m-4gvg, GHSA-rgw5-rvv9-x895), which use the same vector. The reporter self-assessed 6.9 Medium under CVSS 4.0 (`CVSS:4.0/AV:N/AC:L/AT:N/PR:N/UI:N/VC:N/VI:N/VA:L/SC:N/SI:N/SA:N`).

### Credit

Reported by baeseungwon1010, with a working proof of concept and a proposed patch. Vector 2 was identified during maintainer verification.
1240111.title: brace-expansion: DoS via uncontrolled recursion in parseCommaParts causing stack exhaustion

1241209.overview: source-map-js through 1.2.1 fails to validate the per-section offset line value in indexed source maps, allowing attackers to specify arbitrary numeric values. Attackers can supply extremely large offset line values that cause synchronous event loop blocking for extended periods, preventing the service from handling other requests.
1241209.title: source-map-js allows event-loop denial of service through indexed source-map section offsets

1241210.overview:
### Impact

`proxy-addr` determines which network hops are trusted proxies so that `X-Forwarded-For` can be believed. When an application configures a trust subnet as an IPv4-mapped IPv6 address with a short prefix, such as `::ffff:10.0.0.0/8` (the correct spelling is `::ffff:10.0.0.0/104`), the subnet compiles with all-zero leading bits and matches every IPv4 address instead of the block it names. The same happens for any IPv6 trust subnet with zero leading bits, such as `::/1`.

Every unauthenticated client is then trusted as a proxy at hop 0, so `proxyaddr(req, trust)`, and therefore `req.ip` and `req.ips` in Express, returns whatever the client sends in `X-Forwarded-For`. This defeats IP-based access control, rate limiting, geolocation, and audit logging. The misconfiguration compiles without any error, and the same block written correctly behaves correctly, so the difference is not visible from the configuration.

### Patches

Upgrade to `proxy-addr` 2.0.8. An IPv4 address now matches an IPv6 trust subnet only when that subnet is a genuine IPv4-mapped subnet whose prefix covers the mapped marker.

### Workarounds

Write IPv4 trust subnets in plain IPv4 notation (for example `10.0.0.0/8`). If IPv4-mapped IPv6 notation is required, use the full form so the prefix covers the mapped marker (for example `::ffff:10.0.0.0/104` for the `10.0.0.0/8` block).
1241210.title: proxy-addr vulnerable to IP spoofing via IPv4-mapped IPv6 trust subnet

1241257.overview:
## Summary

`fast-copy` traverses values recursively with no bound on depth. Copying a sufficiently deeply-nested value exhausts the JavaScript call stack and throws a native `RangeError: Maximum call stack size exceeded` from inside the library.

## Details

Both `copy` and `copyStrict` recurse once per level of nesting. The value does not need to be circular (circular references were already handled correctly via an internal cache) and it does not need to be large. A plain object nested a few thousand levels deep is only a few
kilobytes of equivalent JSON.

Measured depths at which copying begins to fail (Node.js, V8; the exact ceiling varies with JIT state and the stack available to the environment):

| Call                 | Last depth that copies successfully |
| -------------------- | ----------------------------------- |
| `copy(object)`       | 2811                                |
| `copy(array)`        | 3983                                |
| `copyStrict(object)` | 1874                                |
| `copyStrict(array)`  | 1874                                |

`JSON.parse` is iterative and parses deeply-nested input without difficulty, so a payload that deserializes cleanly can fail in a subsequent `copy` call.

## Impact

The failure is a synchronous, catchable `RangeError` confined to the `copy` call that received the value. There are no memory safety concerns, no data exposure, and no effect on state outside that call. In a typical server the result is a failed request rather than a failed process.

Applications that call `copy` on externally-supplied data, such as request bodies, cached payloads, merged configuration, etc., do not expect a clone helper to throw may surface this as an unhandled error.

## Patches

Fixed in 4.1.0, and backported to 3.1.0 and 2.2.0 so that every major line has a patch available without requiring a breaking upgrade.

Traversal is now bounded by a `maxDepth` option, defaulting to `1000`, which sits below the native limit in standard environments. Exceeding it throws `MaxDepthExceededError`, which carries the limit that was exceeded and extends `RangeError` so existing handling continues to match.

The limit is configurable for consumers with legitimately deep data. On `3.x` and `4.x` it is set when creating a copier:

```js
import { createCopier } from 'fast-copy';

export const copy = createCopier({ maxDepth: 5000 });
```

On `2.x` it is passed per call, and the error is a property of the exported function rather than a named export:

```js
import copy from 'fast-copy';

copy(value, { maxDepth: 5000 });
// detection: error instanceof copy.MaxDepthExceededError
```

In legacy environments without `Object.setPrototypeOf`, `instanceof MaxDepthExceededError` cannot be supported; check `error.name === 'MaxDepthExceededError'` or `error instanceof RangeError` instead.
1241257.title: fast-copy: Stack exhaustion in fast-copy when copying deeply-nested values

1241331.overview:
### Impact

A memory-related vulnerability has been discovered and fixed in the upstream librsvg dependency. When certain runtime-specific conditions apply, this vulnerability can lead to possible remote code execution (RCE) on glibc-based Linux.

### Patches

#### Using prebuilt binaries provided by sharp?

Most people rely on the prebuilt binaries provided by sharp.

Please upgrade sharp to the latest version, currently 0.35.5, which provides librsvg 2.63.2.

#### Using a globally-installed librsvg?

Please ensure you are using the latest librsvg 2.63.2.

### Workarounds

Add the following to your code to prevent sharp from decoding SVG images.
```js
sharp.block({ operation: ["VipsForeignLoadSvg"] });
```

To avoid RCE, ensure you are using a `node` executable binary compiled as a Position Independent Executable (PIE). Most Linux package managers already use this security-hardening feature however be warned that the "official" Node.js binaries do not.
1
1241331.title: sharp : Vulnerability in librsvg dependency CVE-2026-96889

1242600.overview:
### Impact

When `typographer: true` is enabled, specially crafted Markdown can cause quadratic processing time in the smartquotes rule, potentially leading to denial of service in applications processing untrusted input.

Many opening double quotes followed by unmatched closing single quotes cause repeated scans of the entire opener stack. The same issue occurs with the quote types reversed.

The default configuration (`typographer: false`) is not affected, but this option is enabled with high probability.

### Reproduction

```js
import MarkdownIt from 'markdown-it'
import { performance } from 'node:perf_hooks'

const md = new MarkdownIt({ typographer: true })

for (const k of [2000, 4000, 8000, 16000, 32000]) {
  const input = '"a '.repeat(k) + "b' ".repeat(k)
  const start = performance.now()
  md.render(input)
  console.log(input.length, (performance.now() - start).toFixed(1), 'ms')
}
```

Result:

|input size|time|
|-|-|
|12000|18ms|
|24000|47ms|
|48000|115ms|
|96000|428ms|
|192000|1586ms|

### Patches

Fixed in **15.0.2** and **14.3.2**.

### Workarounds

Disable typography with `typographer: false`, or disable only the smartquotes rule:

```js
md.disable('smartquotes')
```
1242600.title: markdown-it: Quadratic complexity in smartquotes with unmatched closing quotes

1242623.overview:
### Summary

`launch-editor` did not escape `%` on Windows when passing an argument to `cmd`. When an environment variable contained a malicious value, it was possible that that content to be executed.

### Impact

Only apps that match all of the following conditions are affected:

- The user uses Windows
- An attacker can place a file with the malicious filename containing `&` or `%`
- Either of
  - An attacker can inject an environment variable with a malicious value
  - An attacker can add a NTFS alternate data stream to the file placed

### Details

Unlike `.sh` files, `.bat` / `.cmd` files on Windows cannot be called directly using [`child_process.spawn`](https://nodejs.org/docs/latest-v24.x/api/child_process.html#child_processspawncommand-args-options) and requires passing them as an argument of `cmd.exe`. To do so, launch-editor escapes the arguments passed to `cmd.exe`. But `launch-editor` did not escape `%` which is used for environment variables.

Because `launch-editor` checks if the argument matches an existing filename, the attack requires the attacker to be able to place a file.

- If the attacker can inject an environment variable as well, they can include the subcommand in the env variable (e.g. set ` &calc.exe ` to `%ENV%`) and call `launchEditor` with `something%ENV%`.
- If the attacker can place a NTFS alternate data stream to the file (e.g. a NTFS alternate data stream named `~-38%calc.exe`), they can call `launchEditor` with `something %CMDCMDLINE:~-38%calc.exe`.
- If the attacker can create a filename containing the `%CD%` and the subcommand (e.g. `&calc.exe `), they can call `launchEditor` with `./%CD%`
1242623.title: launch-editor: escapeCmdArgs() omits % escaping on Windows

1242646.overview:
### Summary

With `html: true`, markdown-it takes quadratic time to parse repeated unterminated HTML constructs inside a paragraph. This affects HTML comments (`<!--`), processing instructions (`<?`), declarations (`<!A`), and CDATA sections (`<![CDATA[`).

An attacker-controlled input of a few hundred kilobytes can block the Node.js event loop for seconds or tens of seconds. The default configuration has HTML disabled, but the `commonmark` preset enables it.

The issue was reported against the published `markdown-it@15.0.2` package on Node.js 20 and reproduced on the current source with Node.js 24.16.0.

### Details

`src/rules_inline/text.ts` treats `<` as a terminator, causing the inline parser to attempt the HTML rule at successive HTML construct openers.

With HTML enabled, `src/rules_inline/html_inline.ts` applies an anchored regular expression to the remaining input:

```js
const match = state.src.slice(pos).match(HTML_TAG_RE)
```

The comment, processing instruction, declaration, and CDATA alternatives in `src/common/html_re.ts` scan the remaining input for their respective terminators: `-->`, `?>`, `>`, and `]]>`.

When the terminator is absent, matching fails. Parsing eventually reaches the next opener and scans an overlapping suffix again. Repeating this across the paragraph produces quadratic total work. For these inputs, the problem is repeated scanning across separate matches.

The payload must reach inline parsing. Prefixing it with `x ` keeps it inside a paragraph. Starting a line directly with one of these constructs instead invokes HTML block parsing, which does not exhibit the same repeated inline scans for these payloads.

The existing `unclosed <!--` test in `test/markdown-it/pathological.test.mjs` already contains a reproducer:

```js
'</' + '<!--'.repeat(100000)
```

However, it runs with default options, where HTML is disabled.

A fix should avoid repeated searches for absent terminators across all four affected alternatives, for example by caching failed searches on the inline state. Fixing only the comment alternative leaves the other three cases affected. Regression coverage should exercise all four with `html: true`.

The original report was submitted by [@JarLob](https://github.com/JarLob). It credits the [GitHub Security Lab Taskflow Agent](https://github.com/GitHubSecurityLab/seclab-taskflow-agent) as part of the [GitHub Secure Open Source Fund](https://github.com/open-source/github-secure-open-source-fund).

### Proof of concept

Install the affected package in an empty directory:

```sh
npm install markdown-it@15.0.2
```

Save the following as `poc.mjs` and run `node poc.mjs`:

```js
import MarkdownIt from 'markdown-it'
import { performance } from 'node:perf_hooks'

const mdHtml = new MarkdownIt({ html: true })
const mdDefault = new MarkdownIt()
const sizes = [8000, 16000, 32000, 64000]

function measure(md, src) {
  const start = performance.now()
  md.render(src)
  return (performance.now() - start).toFixed(1)
}

const variants = {
  comment: '<!--',
  processing: '<?x',
  declaration: '<!A',
  cdata: '<![CDATA['
}

for (const [name, opener] of Object.entries(variants)) {
  console.log(`\n${name}`)
  for (const n of sizes) {
    const src = 'x ' + opener.repeat(n)
    console.log({
      n,
      bytes: Buffer.byteLength(src),
      ms: measure(mdHtml, src)
    })
  }
}

const n = sizes.at(-1)
const controls = {
  'HTML disabled': [mdDefault, 'x ' + '<!--'.repeat(n)],
  'Closed comments': [mdHtml, 'x ' + '<!---->'.repeat(n)],
  'HTML block': [mdHtml, '<!--'.repeat(n)],
  'Plain text': [mdHtml, 'x ' + 'abcd'.repeat(n)]
}

for (const [name, [md, src]] of Object.entries(controls)) {
  console.log({ control: name, ms: measure(md, src) })
}

const repoPayload = '</' + '<!--'.repeat(100000)
console.log({
  payload: 'Existing pathological test',
  htmlFalseMs: measure(mdDefault, repoPayload),
  htmlTrueMs: measure(mdHtml, repoPayload)
})
```

Measurements from the original report on `markdown-it@15.0.2`, Node.js 20:

| Construct | 8,000 repetitions | 64,000 repetitions |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| Comment | 170 ms | 8,799 ms |
| Processing instruction | 26 ms | 1,566 ms |
| Declaration | 93 ms | 5,628 ms |
| CDATA | 119 ms | 4,179 ms |

An eightfold increase in repetitions produces approximately 35ÔÇô60 times the execution time, consistent with quadratic growth becoming dominant.

For the comment payload at 64,000 repetitions:

- HTML disabled: 25 ms.
- Closed comments: 29 ms.
- Payload at the start of an HTML block: 1 ms.
- Plain text: 1 ms.

The existing pathological-test payload with 100,000 comment openers took 33 ms with HTML disabled and 21,030 ms with HTML enabled. A separate comment payload with 128,000 repetitions, approximately 500 KiB, took 32,847 ms.

Exact timings depend on the runtime and hardware.

### Impact

This is an availability issue affecting applications that render attacker-controlled Markdown with `html: true`, including applications using the `commonmark` preset.

On Node.js, a synchronous `render()` call can occupy a CPU core and block the event loop for seconds or tens of seconds, delaying other requests handled by the same process. Repeated submissions can cause denial of service. Browser applications can similarly become unresponsive when rendering on the main thread.

Sanitizing the generated HTML afterwards does not prevent the issue because the expensive processing occurs during Markdown rendering.

The default configuration, with HTML disabled, is unaffected by these payloads. Disabling HTML or limiting input size can reduce exposure while a fix is prepared.

The reported affected release is `15.0.2`; the full affected version range has not been established.
1242646.title: markdown-it: Quadratic-time denial of service in inline HTML parsing with html enabled

1242652.overview:
### Summary

`launch-editor` forwarded file paths directly to editors without sanitization. If a path resembles a CLI flag, editors like Vim may interpret it as a command, potentially causing unintended file overwrites or command execution.

### Impact

#### Direct `launch-editor` users

Only apps that match all of the following conditions are affected:

- The attacker is able to create a file system entry (e.g. a file or directory) starting with `+` or `-` in the working directory
- The user uses or the app specifies any of the following editors:
  - Vim (including gVim)
  - MacVim
  - Emacs (including Emacsclient)
  - Notepad++ (only if using a plugin exposing dangerous operations via plugin messages)
- The first argument of `launchEditor` can start with `+` or `-` or the user is using WSL

#### `launch-editor-middleware` users

Only apps that match the following conditions are affected:

- The attacker is able to create a file system entry (e.g. a file or directory) starting with `+` or `-` in the working directory
- The user uses or the app specifies any of the following editors:
  - Vim (including gVim)
  - MacVim
  - Emacs (including Emacsclient)
  - Notepad++ (only if using a plugin exposing dangerous operations via plugin messages)
- launch-editor older than v2.2.0 is used, or the user is using WSL

#### Vite users

Only apps that match the following conditions are affected:

- The attacker is able to create a file system entry (e.g. a file or directory) starting with `+` or `-` in the working directory
- The user uses or the app specifies any of the following editors:
  - Vim (including gVim)
  - MacVim
  - Emacs (including Emacsclient)
  - Notepad++ (only if using a plugin exposing dangerous operations via plugin messages)
- The user is using WSL

### Details

`launchEditor(file)` function passes the file name as-is to the editor if the file with that file name exists. If the file name starts with `-` (also `+` for Vim), the editor treats them as flags rather than positional arguments. For example, Vim treats arguments starting with `+` as an Ex command. As a result, an existing relative directory such as:
```
+call writefile(["SAFE_MARKER"],"LAUNCH_EDITOR_MARKER")|qa!
```
is not treated as a filename when passed to Vim. Vim executes the embedded Ex command.

The following editor has a potentially destructive operation exposed to the CLI arguments:
- Vim (including gVim)
- MacVim
- Emacs (including Emacsclient)
- Notepad++ (only if using a plugin exposing dangerous operations via plugin messages)

`launch-editor-middleware` v2.2.0+ converts the passed file path to an absolute path so those are not affected as long as the user is not using WSL. For WSL, `launch-editor` converts the paths to relative paths internally, so those are still affected.

Vite 2.0.0+ uses `launch-editor-middleware` v2.2.0+ so the WSL users are only affected.
1242652.title: launch-editor: Editor CLI flag misinterpretation causing arbitrary command execution for some editors

1242659.overview:
### Summary

`launch-editor` checked `fs.existsSync(fileName)` before passing a supplied path to an editor command. On Windows, an attacker can bypass this check with a crafted path ending in `\\..:line:column`. This removes the requirement that the attacker be able to place a file with a malicious filename.

Combined with the `%` escaping issue described in [GHSA-698v-4r3x-3vcv](https://github.com/vitejs/launch-editor/security/advisories/GHSA-698v-4r3x-3vcv), this bypass can lead to OS command injection when an attacker controls the file argument.

### Impact

Only apps that runs on Windows is affected.

### Details

The earlier advisory assumed that `fs.existsSync()` required an attacker-controlled filename to exist. This advisory covers a bypass of that requirement.

A crafted value ending in `\\..:1:1` is interpreted differently by `launch-editor-middleware`, `launch-editor`, and Windows:

1. `launch-editor-middleware` calls `path.resolve()` while the final path component is `..:1:1`, so it is not treated as a parent-directory component.
2. `launch-editor` treats `:1:1` as a line-and-column suffix and removes it, leaving a path ending in `\\..`.
3. On Windows, `fs.existsSync()` accepts the resulting path as the existing parent directory even though the attacker-controlled preceding component does not exist.
4. Because the existence check passes, the crafted filename reaches the Windows shell command.
1242659.title: launch-editor: `fs.existsSync()` existence check can be bypassed on Windows

1242672.title: markdown-it: Quadratic-time rendering of a single multi-line link reference definition with default options (regression since 14.0)

1242725.title: Vite: Cross origin script execution through Vite custom middleware

1242731.overview:
### Summary

The content of files outside `server.fs` setting can be returned to the browser if the project imports a file path concatenated with the `root`. For example, if the project references `<path-to-project-root>/etc/hosts`, the content of `/etc/hosts` was possible to be returned.

The content of files outside the `server.fs.allow` option can be returned to the browser when a project imports a file whose root-relative path matches an absolute path on the host. For example, referencing `<project-root>/etc/hosts` could make Vite return the host's `/etc/hosts` file.

### Impact

Only apps that meet all of the following conditions are affected:

- explicitly expose the Vite dev server to the network (using `--host` or the [`server.host` option](https://vite.dev/config/server-options#server-host))
- contain an imported file whose root-relative browser URL is also the absolute path of a readable file on the host
- The sensitive file is not matched by [`server.fs.deny`](https://vite.dev/config/server-options#server-fs-deny)
- the dev server is not running on Windows

### Details

When Vite analyzes an in-root import, it rewrites the resolved module ID to a browser URL such as `/etc/hostname`. In affected versions, Vite converts that URL with `fsPathFromUrl` and adds the result to `safeModulePaths`. Because `fsPathFromUrl` ensures a leading slash without resolving the URL against the project root, the project URL `/etc/hostname` is recorded as if it were the absolute filesystem path `/etc/hostname`.

For a later request to `/@fs/etc/hostname`, the raw-filesystem middleware interprets `/etc/hostname` as an absolute path. The access check applies `server.fs.deny`, then accepts paths present in `safeModulePaths` before checking `server.fs.allow`. As a result, the request can return the host file instead of the project file that originally populated `safeModulePaths`.

### PoC
The following example requires Linux with a readable `/etc/hostname`:
```bash
$ mkdir vite-safe-module-path-poc
$ cd vite-safe-module-path-poc
$ npm init -y
$ npm install vite@8.3.1
$ mkdir -p etc
$ echo 'PROJECT-DECOY\n' > etc/hostname
$ echo 'import "./etc/hostname"\n' > main.js
$ npx vite --host 127.0.0.1
```

In another terminal:
```bash
$ curl -o /dev/null -s -w '%{http_code}\n' http://127.0.0.1:5173/main.js
200
$ curl -sS -o response -w '%{http_code}\n' http://127.0.0.1:5173/@fs/etc/hostname
200
$ cmp -s response /etc/hostname && echo 'response matches host file'
response matches host file
```
1242731.title: Vite: Files outside `server.fs.allow` could be served when project paths match system paths on non-Windows machine

1242883.title: ip-address: Address6 matches a zone identifier in quadratic time ahead of its length limit, allowing a single long string to stall the process

1243066.overview: Zod schema-validation library through 4.6.5 contains an uncontrolled resource consumption vulnerability that allows attackers to exhaust memory by submitting a large array to an application using an array schema without a length constraint. Attackers can exploit the handleArrayResult parse logic in $ZodArray, which accumulates every validation issue for each failing element with no cap or early termination, causing the process to allocate excessive issue objects and crash due to out-of-memory conditions.
1243066.title: Zod can exhaust memory while validating oversized constrained collections

1243074.overview:
### Impact

A single request can crash any application using `body-parser` with default options. When a request carries a `Content-Encoding` (for example `gzip`), `body-parser` pipes it into a decompression stream and, after reading the body, leaves that stream piped with no error listener. A payload of one valid compressed frame followed by trailing bytes decodes and the application responds normally, but the trailing bytes then reach the already-finished decoder, which emits an error that is re-thrown as an uncaught exception and terminates the process. No authentication or matching route is required, since parsing runs before routing.

### Patches

Fixed in body-parser 2.4.0 and 1.20.9. Upgrade to one of these versions.

### Workarounds

Pass `inflate: false` to the body-parser middleware if the application does not need to accept compressed request bodies. This rejects encoded requests before any decompression stream is created.
1243074.title: body-parser vulnerable to Denial of Service via trailing bytes after a compressed request body

1243083.overview:
### Impact

When `multer` is configured with an asynchronous `fileFilter`, a single request can crash the Node.js process. If a request is aborted (for example when one file is rejected) while another file's async `fileFilter` is still pending, the pending callback later resumes a parsing stream that multer has already torn down. busboy then emits an error on a stream that no longer has an error listener, which Node raises as an unhandled `'error'` event, and the process exits. A single unauthenticated request is enough, so any application using `multer` with an asynchronous `fileFilter` is affected, regardless of storage engine. Uploads using a synchronous `fileFilter` are not affected.

### Patches

Users should upgrade to `multer` `2.5.0` or later.

### Workarounds

Use a synchronous `fileFilter`.
1243083.title: multer vulnerable to Denial of Service via a pending asynchronous fileFilter after request teardown

1243097.overview:
### Impact

`fast-uri` percent-decodes the scheme component with the legacy global `unescape()` before validating it, so an input whose decoded scheme is a valid but dangerous token is emitted as a live scheme. RFC 3986 section 3.1 does not allow percent-encoding in a scheme, so no RFC or WHATWG parser treats such input as having that scheme, but `fast-uri` does.

For example, `normalize('%6Aavascript:alert(1)')` returns `javascript:alert(1)`, `resolve('https://a.example/', '%6Aavascript:alert(1)')` returns `javascript:alert(1)`, and `parse('%6Aavascript:alert(1)').scheme` returns `javascript`. The `%uXXXX` form (`%u006Aavascript:`) produces the same result, and `equal('%68ttp://a/', 'http://a/')` returns `true`.

An application that screens dangerous schemes on the raw input and then stores or renders `normalize(input)` or `resolve(base, input)` turns an inert string into an executable `javascript:`, `data:`, or `vbscript:` URL, a stored or reflected cross-site scripting vector in the consuming application. `equal()` also treats an encoded and a plain scheme as the same, which can bypass equality-based allowlists.

### Patches

Upgrade to `fast-uri` `2.4.8`, `3.1.9`, or `4.2.3`.

### Workarounds

Reject input whose scheme part (before the first `:`, and before any `/`, `?`, or `#`) contains `%`. Alternatively, check `parse(x).scheme` against an allowlist after normalization and use that same parsed result rather than the raw string.
1243097.title: fast-uri vulnerable to URI scheme spoofing via percent-encoded scheme decoding

1243100.overview:
### Impact

`fast-uri`'s `normalize()` and `serialize()` apply RFC 3986 dot-segment removal (`remove_dot_segments`) to the path of a relative-path reference. RFC 3986 section 5.2.4 defines that algorithm only for the merged target path during resolution, not for the reference itself, so applied to the reference it drops leading `..` segments and can turn a document-relative reference into a root-relative one.

For example, `normalize('a/../b')` returns `/b` and `normalize('../x')` returns `x`, so `resolve(base, normalize(ref))` points at a different resource than `resolve(base, ref)`, and `equal()` treats distinct references as the same.

Applications that normalize attacker-supplied or user-supplied relative references and then resolve them, or use them as cache, deduplication, or authorization keys, can have a reference escape its intended directory and point at a different resource.

### Patches

Upgrade to `fast-uri` `2.4.8`, `3.1.9`, or `4.2.3`.

### Workarounds

Do not normalize a relative reference before resolving it. Resolve it against the absolute base first, then normalize the absolute result.
1243100.title: fast-uri vulnerable to improper path equivalence in relative reference normalization

1243103.overview:
### Impact

`fast-uri` versions `>= 2.4.2, <= 2.4.7`, `>= 3.1.3, <= 3.1.8`, and `>= 4.0.1, <= 4.2.2` can silently rewrite the host of an HTTP-family URL (`http`, `https`, `ws`, `wss`, or any scheme with `domainHost: true`). For those schemes `canonicalizeHost()` passes the parsed host to the WHATWG `URL` parser and adopts its `.hostname` without checking that the parser read the whole input as a host. RFC 3986 permits `@` inside the host group and the WHATWG parser strips TAB, LF, and CR, so the authority `fast-uri` reports is rewritten by that second parser with no `error` set: data before an `@` is dropped and whitespace is removed.

For example, `fast-uri` parses `http://a@b@evil.example/` to host `evil.example` (dropping the `b` segment), and a host containing a raw TAB, CR, or LF has those characters stripped. `equal()` then treats a whitespace-smuggled host as the same as the clean one, and `resolve()` rewrites the authority the same way.

Applications that use `fast-uri` to enforce host-based policy (denylists, loopback filtering, redirect validation, outbound proxy routing) on one representation, such as the raw input, see a policy/use desync: the canonical host `fast-uri` returns differs from what was checked, and traffic can be steered to an unintended destination.

### Patches

Upgrade to `fast-uri` `2.4.8`, `3.1.9`, or `4.2.3`.

### Workarounds

Reject URIs whose authority contains more than one `@`, or contains TAB, CR, or LF, before calling `fast-uri`. Alternatively, treat any non-empty `parse(x).error` as fatal, and compare hosts only from the same `parse()` result.
1243103.title: fast-uri vulnerable to host confusion via unchecked WHATWG host canonicalization

1243106.overview:
### Impact

`fast-uri`'s `serialize()`, `normalize()`, and `resolve()`, when called with the non-default option `reference: 'suffix'` on a reference that has no authority, emit a relative reference whose first path segment contains a bare colon without escaping it. RFC 3986 section 3.3 requires the first segment of a `path-noscheme` reference not to contain a colon, precisely because a bare colon makes the string reparse as an absolute URI with a scheme. `fast-uri`'s default serialization escapes that colon, but the suffix path does not.

For example, `normalize('javascript:alert(1)', { reference: 'suffix' })` returns `javascript:alert(1)`, which reparses as a live `javascript:` scheme; `data:` and `vbscript:` behave the same.

Applications that serialize or normalize a relative reference with `reference: 'suffix'` and then treat the result as a URI can turn inert input into a live `javascript:`, `data:`, or `vbscript:` URL (a cross-site scripting vector), and `equal()` can conflate a scheme-bearing reference with a relative one. Exposure is limited to applications that use the non-default `reference: 'suffix'` option.

### Patches

Upgrade to `fast-uri` `2.4.8`, `3.1.9`, or `4.2.3`.

### Workarounds

Do not use the `reference: 'suffix'` option on untrusted input. If suffix output is required, percent-encode a colon in the first path segment of the result before treating it as a URI.
1243106.title: fast-uri vulnerable to scheme injection via an unescaped first-segment colon in suffix references

1243379.overview:
### Impact

`.` and `#` are not word delimiters in the tokenizer, so a flat selector such as
`.a.a.a...` reaches `splitWord()` as a single word token carrying n class or id
indexes. Three passes scanned those index arrays linearly for every index,
making the parse O(n^2) in the number of indexes rather than in input length:
`uniqs()`, the `indices.forEach` loop, and the Sass-interpolation filter.
Parsing a 400 KB flat selector took ~34 s on a modern laptop, fully occupying a
single thread. A benign selector of identical byte size parses in tens of
milliseconds, so the cost is driven by the index count, not the input size.
The nesting depth of such a selector is 0, so the `maxNestingDepth` guard added
in 7.1.3 offers no protection.

Reachability is deployment dependent. Only consumers that parse untrusted,
attacker-supplied selectors synchronously in a request path are exposed, for
example CSS sanitizers, CSS-in-JS services and online playgrounds. Ordinary
build-time use on trusted sources is not affected.

### Patches

Fixed in 7.1.6. The three passes now use Set membership tests, making parsing
linear in the number of indexes. There is no behaviour change: parsing is
byte-identical on a differential corpus of 8413 selectors.

### Workarounds

Cap the size of selectors accepted from untrusted sources before parsing.
1243379.title: PostCSS: Quadratic complexity in flat selector parsing allows CPU exhaustion

1243687.overview:
## Summary

`qs.stringify(obj, { arrayFormat: 'comma' })` throws an uncaught `TypeError: Cannot convert object to primitive value` when an array in `obj` contains an element that carries an own, non-callable `toString` property (for example `{ a: [ { toString: 'x' } ] }`). A remote, unauthenticated attacker who can influence an object that the application later re-serializes with the comma array format triggers the throw. In a service that lacks a synchronous error boundary around the serialization call, the uncaught exception crashes the worker process, producing a denial of service.

## Root Cause

When `arrayFormat: 'comma'` is selected, the comma branch collapses the whole array into a single value via `Array.prototype.join`, or, under `encodeValuesOnly: true`, maps each element through the value encoder before joining. Both paths perform an implicit string coercion (`ToPrimitive` with hint `"string"`) on each element. For an object whose own `toString` is a non-callable value, coercion skips the shadowed non-callable `toString`, falls through to `Object.prototype.valueOf` (which returns the object rather than a primitive), and throws. The comma branch runs this coercion before the per-element null and skip handling in the main loop, so nothing downstream can neutralize the hostile element, and the throw is never caught inside the library.

```text
lib/stringify.js  (comma-array branch)
  line 152-154: obj = utils.maybeMap(obj, function (v) { return v == null ? v : encoder(v); });  // encodeValuesOnly path
  line 156:     objKeys = [{ value: obj.length > 0 ? obj.join(',') || null : void undefined }];   // default comma path
lib/utils.js
  line 292:     string = String(str);   // value encoder coercion reached via the encodeValuesOnly path
```

## Impact

Prerequisites: the application calls `qs.stringify` with `arrayFormat: 'comma'` (a documented, supported option) on an object whose shape can be influenced by attacker input. Attacker-controllable sources include `qs.parse(input, { allowPrototypes: true })`, which retains a `toString` segment (Express 4's default query parser, Express 5's `extended` query parser, and body-parser's `extended` urlencoded parser all set it), `qs.parse(input, { plainObjects: true })`, whose null-prototype elements throw even without a `toString` key (eg, `a[][b]=c`), and `JSON.parse` of a request body, which needs no qs parse option at all. No authentication or user interaction is required. Demonstrated capability: a single request forces an uncaught synchronous `TypeError` in the serialization call. In a naive single-process Node service with no synchronous error boundary, this crashes the process and takes the service offline (availability impact). Under a framework such as Express that traps synchronous handler throws, the plausible outcome is a per-request 500 rather than a full outage; that lower-impact case is noted but not the worst credible supported deployment. There is no confidentiality or integrity impact, no memory unsafety, and no prototype pollution.

## Proof of Concept

`Install qs at the affected version (for example 6.16.0) and run the following script with Node.js. No network setup is required; it demonstrates the throw in isolation.`

```js
var qs = require('qs');

// Source A: qs.parse with allowPrototypes retains the hostile toString segment
qs.stringify(qs.parse('a[0][toString]=x', { allowPrototypes: true }), { arrayFormat: 'comma' });

// Source B: a JSON request body, no qs parse option needed
qs.stringify(JSON.parse('{"a":[{"toString":"x"}]}'), { arrayFormat: 'comma' });

// Also affected: the encodeValuesOnly sub-path
qs.stringify(JSON.parse('{"a":[{"toString":"x"}]}'), { arrayFormat: 'comma', encodeValuesOnly: true });
```

```text
A default-join (allowPrototypes) => THREW: TypeError: Cannot convert object to primitive value
B default-join (JSON.parse) => THREW: TypeError: Cannot convert object to primitive value
C encodeValuesOnly path => THREW: TypeError: Cannot convert object to primitive value
N2 callable toString => NO THROW; output="a=z"
N3 isBuffer vector (CVE-2026-82417) => NO THROW; output="a%5Bconstructor%5D%5BisBuffer%5D=x"
qs version: 6.16.0
```

## Attack Chain

1. **Exposure:** A remote, unauthenticated request reaches an endpoint whose handler eventually serializes attacker-influenced data with `qs.stringify(obj, { arrayFormat: 'comma' })`.
2. **Control:** The attacker supplies data that becomes `{ a: [ { toString: <non-callable value> } ] }`, either via `a[0][toString]=x` parsed with `allowPrototypes`, or via a JSON body `{"a":[{"toString":"x"}]}`.
3. **Path:** In `stringify`, the primitive/buffer guard at `lib/stringify.js:134` is false for an array, so control reaches the comma branch at `lib/stringify.js:149`.
4. **Guard:** On the `encodeValuesOnly` path, the closure `v == null ? v : encoder(v)` at `lib/stringify.js:152-154` passes only `null`/`undefined` through; a non-null object still reaches the encoder. The default path skips that closure entirely and reaches `obj.join(',')` at `lib/stringify.js:156` with no guard at all.
5. **Primitive:** The element is coerced to a string (`Array.prototype.join`, or `String(str)` at `lib/utils.js:292`). `ToPrimitive` skips the non-callable own `toString`, `valueOf` returns the object, and a `TypeError` is thrown.
6. **Result:** The uncaught synchronous exception propagates out of the serialization call, failing the request and, in a service without a synchronous error boundary, crashing the process (denial of service).

## Bypass Evidence

This is a different element type on the code path CVE-2026-8723 (GHSA-q8mj-m7cp-5q26) patched, plus the default comma path, which that fix never covered. CVE-2026-8723 addressed a `TypeError` crash on `null`/`undefined` entries in the comma plus `encodeValuesOnly` path. Its fix (commit 21f80b3) wraps the encoder in `function (v) { return v == null ? v : encoder(v); }`, so it only passes `null` and `undefined` through. A non-null element with a hostile own `toString` fails the `v == null` test, so the encoder still runs and still throws; the encodeValuesOnly case (case C above) throws on the exact fixed code. The default comma path (`encodeValuesOnly` unset, the library default) never entered that fix at all: `git log -S "obj.join(','" -- lib/stringify.js` shows no security fix has ever touched the `obj.join(',')` line, and cases A and B throw with `encodeValuesOnly` unset. The related isBuffer hardening for CVE-2026-82417 (commit e83d321) is a different sink at the `lib/stringify.js:134` guard, which is never entered for the array element; the negative control `{a:{constructor:{isBuffer:'x'}}}` serializes cleanly. Disproof attempts that failed: a `valueOf`-only object does not throw (it serializes to `[object Object]`), confirming the trigger is an element with no callable `toString` (an own non-callable `toString`, or a null-prototype object with no `toString` at all, as `qs.parse` produces under `plainObjects`); nested arrays (`{"a":[[{"toString":"x"}]]}`) throw the same way; a callable `toString` serializes cleanly; and the default (non-comma) array format serializes cleanly, confirming the comma format is required. All positive and negative cases were reproduced on the exact published 6.16.0 artifact.

## Affected Versions

- `Ecosystem: npm`
- `Package: qs`
- `Confirmed affected range: >= 6.7.0, <= 6.16.0`
- `Latest release checked: 6.16.0 (npm latest; git tag v6.16.0)`
- `Fix status: fixed in 6.16.1 (a952e75)`

The `arrayFormat: 'comma'` join sink was introduced in qs 6.7.0, so 6.7.0 is the lower boundary; releases before 6.7.0 lack the sink. No released version fixes this vector, and the latest published release (6.16.0) reproduces the throw, so the closed upper bound `<= 6.16.0` covers every affected release. The `encodeValuesOnly` sub-path was added later, but the default comma-join vector already affects 6.7.0, so 6.7.0 governs the lower boundary.

## Suggested Fix

The comma array serialization must not allow an implicit string coercion of an array element to throw an uncaught exception. Coercion of each comma element should be performed defensively (for example by wrapping the join and per-element encode so that a coercion failure is caught and handled), and this protection must cover both the default `obj.join(',')` path and the `encodeValuesOnly` encoder path, not only the previously patched `null`/`undefined` case. As an interim mitigation without a code change, applications can avoid `arrayFormat: 'comma'` when serializing data derived from untrusted input, sanitize parsed objects (avoid `allowPrototypes`/`plainObjects` on untrusted input and strip unexpected own properties), or wrap `qs.stringify` calls in a synchronous error boundary so a coercion failure cannot crash the process.

Reported by zx (GitHub: @manus-pi).

---

## Independent report by @Lucidsec

The following was reported separately, after this advisory, and is merged here as a duplicate.

### Summary

In project [qs](https://github.com/ljharb/qs), in versions `>= 6.7.0, <= 6.16.0` (every version that supports `arrayFormat: 'comma'`), `qs.stringify` with `arrayFormat: 'comma'` can throw an uncaught `TypeError: Cannot convert object to primitive value` when an array element has a non-callable own `toString`. It is fixed in 6.16.1. Related: CWE-248 and CWE-704.

### Technical Details

`qs.stringify` with `arrayFormat: 'comma'` joins an array at `lib/stringify.js:156` via `obj.join(',')`. An element whose own `toString` is not callable makes `Array.prototype.join` throw. There is no type check and no catch on that path.

A second path exists with `encodeValuesOnly`: at `lib/stringify.js:151-154`, `maybeMap` only skips `v == null`, then `lib/utils.js:292` does `String(str)` and throws the same `TypeError` (this second site exists since v6.11.1; before that, the same input throws at `join`).

Who can trigger: someone who can shape an array element passed to `stringify`. The host must use non-default `arrayFormat: 'comma'`. Default `arrayFormat` `indices` does not fold arrays and is not affected. A parse-then-stringify path also needs `plainObjects: true` (null-prototype elements from `lib/parse.js:200`) or `allowPrototypes: true` (which Express 4's default query parser, Express 5's `extended` query parser, and body-parser's `extended` urlencoded parser all set). Default `qs.parse('a[0][toString]=x')` returns `{}` because the prototype guard drops `toString`. Direct JSON handed to `stringify` can supply `{"a":[{"toString":"x"}]}`.

Cause: the comma fold at `lib/stringify.js:149-156` collapses the array into a single value before the main loop at `lib/stringify.js:172-212`, so `skipNulls` and `strictNullHandling` only ever see the joined value, never individual elements. `isNonNullishPrimitive` / `isBuffer` at `lib/stringify.js:134` inspect the whole value, not each element. A normal object uses `Object.prototype.toString` and becomes `[object Object]`. An own non-callable `toString` is skipped, `valueOf` returns the object, and `join` throws. (The skipped TODO test at `test/stringify.js:684-689` uses a plain `{ b: 1 }` element, which does not throw; it covers the separate question of what comma format should output for object elements, not this crash.) Earlier comma crash fixes did not cover object elements.

### Impact

One small input makes that serialization path throw a synchronous, catchable `TypeError`. Behind a framework error boundary (eg, a synchronous Express handler), the request fails with a 500 and the process survives. In a host with no error boundary (eg, a bare `http.createServer` handler), the uncaught exception exits the process (the client sees `ECONNRESET`). Availability only.

### Proof of Concept

<details>
<summary>Show the proof of concept</summary>

Checked on the latest commit that was checked: `07b1d4d82c8f9301c105ea4b94fa2302cfd6e8b4`. Still present. Demonstrated.

- Payload `{"a":[{"toString":"x"}]}` throws at `lib/stringify.js:156`.
- Baseline `{"a":["x","y"]}` returns 200 with body `a=x%2Cy`.
- A plain object element stringifies to `a=%5Bobject%20Object%5D` and does not throw.
- `encodeValuesOnly: true` throws via `utils.js:292`.
- `plainObjects` parse plus comma throws.

</details>

### Suggested Fix

Before `join`, map elements with the existing primitive check; skip or replace non-primitives so `join` cannot throw. On the `encodeValuesOnly` path, do not send non-primitives into `String()`. Optionally guard `lib/utils.js:292`. Add new regression tests.

1244623.overview:
minimatch 10.2.6 contains an attacker-controlled pattern amplification in firstPhasePreProcess() when optimizationLevel >= 2.

researcher: Reid Downing (b1nv0id)
files: 

- src/index.ts: 690-770
- src/index.ts: 780-796

issue:
input-controlled growth of globParts during first-phase preprocessing, followed by quadratic second-phase processing.

the **/../ transformation clones a globparts entry and appends the clone to the same globparts array:
```
parts.splice(gs, 1)
const other = parts.slice(0)
other[gs] = '**'
globParts.push(other)
```
this occurs inside a do...while (didSomething) fixpoint loop, allowing generated entries to be processed again.

the expanded globparts array is subsequently processed by secondPhasePreProcess(), which performs pairwise comparisons:
```
for (let i = 0; i < globParts.length - 1; i++) {
  for (let j = i + 1; j < globParts.length; j++) {
    this.partsMatch(...)
  }
}
```
an attacker who can supply a glob pattern can therefore cause additional pattern entries to be generated during preprocessing, followed by quadratic pairwise processing, resulting in excessive cpu and memory consumption.
